reference_sources.summary: The ILO explanation of Convention 29 links forced labour to work or service, menace of a penalty and involuntariness. Voluntary participation concerns informed consent and practical freedom to leave. Cross-border movement is not an element of this definition. Its stated exceptions and the evidence supporting each element require attention.
reference_sources.source_kind: ILO explanation of an international labour convention
reference_sources.scope: Assess the elements of the standard separately from the facts needed for a domestic criminal finding.

reference_sources.summary: The ILO fair-recruitment principles and definition of recruitment fees and related costs place recruitment costs away from workers: workers should bear neither direct nor indirect recruitment charges. Assess actual cost allocation, including required training or medical services, rather than the payment label alone.
reference_sources.scope: Use as the stated international fair-recruitment benchmark. Distinguish that benchmark from a jurisdiction-specific offence and examine any applicable exception and fee category.

reference_sources.summary: Convention 181 Article 7 sets a rule against private employment agencies charging workers recruitment fees or costs. Article 7(2) permits competent-authority exceptions in workers' interests, after representative employer/worker consultation, for specified categories of workers and services. A worker's signature alone is not that exception.
reference_sources.scope: Ratification, territorial application and domestic implementation affect binding obligations. The text still supplies a defined standard against which the arrangement can be discussed.

reference_sources.summary: Convention 95 Article 6 protects workers' freedom to dispose of wages. Article 8 addresses permitted deduction conditions and disclosure. Article 9 prohibits wage deductions that pay employers or intermediaries for obtaining or retaining employment. This differs from a blanket ban on every deduction, such as authorized taxes.
reference_sources.scope: Identify the payment's actual purpose and applicable treaty/domestic scope. Consent or a financing label alone does not resolve job-access deductions or wage-control concerns.

reference_sources.summary: The revised ILO indicator guide supports identifying coercion and lack of consent through the facts of a situation. Relevant questions include document access, control of earned wages, threats, recruitment debt and ability to leave. Indicators guide protective inquiry and referral; evaluate their combination and context.
reference_sources.scope: Risk recognition, immediate protective steps and a categorical offence finding are separate assessments.

reference_sources.summary: The ILO explanation of Convention 29 links forced labour to work or service, menace of a penalty and involuntariness. Voluntary participation concerns informed consent and practical freedom to leave. Cross-border movement is not an element of this definition. Its stated exceptions and the evidence supporting each element require attention.

reference_sources.summary: The ILO fair-recruitment principles and definition of recruitment fees and related costs place recruitment costs away from workers: workers should bear neither direct nor indirect recruitment charges. Assess actual cost allocation, including required training or medical services, rather than the payment label alone.
reference_sources.scope: Use as the stated international fair-recruitment benchmark. Distinguish that benchmark from a jurisdiction-specific offence and examine any applicable exception and fee category.

reference_sources.summary: Convention 181 Article 7 sets a rule against private employment agencies charging workers recruitment fees or costs. Article 7(2) permits competent-authority exceptions in workers' interests, after representative employer/worker consultation, for specified categories of workers and services. A worker's signature alone is not that exception.
reference_sources.scope: Ratification, territorial application and domestic implementation affect binding obligations. The text still supplies a defined standard against which the arrangement can be discussed.

reference_sources.summary: Convention 95 Article 6 protects workers' freedom to dispose of wages. Article 8 addresses permitted deduction conditions and disclosure. Article 9 prohibits wage deductions that pay employers or intermediaries for obtaining or retaining employment. This differs from a blanket ban on every deduction, such as authorized taxes.
reference_sources.scope: Identify the payment's actual purpose and applicable treaty/domestic scope. Consent or a financing label alone does not resolve job-access deductions or wage-control concerns.

reference_sources.summary: The revised ILO indicator guide supports identifying coercion and lack of consent through the facts of a situation. Relevant questions include document access, control of earned wages, threats, recruitment debt and ability to leave. Indicators guide protective inquiry and referral; evaluate their combination and context.
reference_sources.scope: Risk recognition, immediate protective steps and a categorical offence finding are separate assessments.

A worker's signature alone is not that exception.
reference_sources.scope: Ratification, territorial application and domestic implementation affect binding obligations. The text still supplies a defined standard against which the arrangement can be discussed.

reference_sources.summary: Convention 95 Article 6 protects workers' freedom to dispose of wages. Article 8 addresses permitted deduction conditions and disclosure. Article 9 prohibits wage deductions that pay employers or intermediaries for obtaining or retaining employment. This differs from a blanket ban on every deduction, such as authorized taxes.
reference_sources.scope: Identify the payment's actual purpose and applicable treaty/domestic scope. Consent or a financing label alone does not resolve job-access deductions or wage-control concerns.

reference_sources.summary: The revised ILO indicator guide supports identifying coercion and lack of consent through the facts of a situation. Relevant questions include document access, control of earned wages, threats, recruitment debt and ability to leave. Indicators guide protective inquiry and referral; evaluate their combination and context.
reference_sources.scope: Risk recognition, immediate protective steps and a categorical offence finding are separate assessments.
